questions.stem: The probability density function $f(x)$ of a random variable $X$ which takes real values is $$f(x)=\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\left(-\frac{x^2}{18}\right),\quad x\in(-\infty,+\infty)$$ Which one of the following statements is correct about the random variable $X$?

steps.title: What the density tells you
steps.body: A probability density function (pdf) $f(x)$ describes a continuous random variable: the chance that $X$ lands in a range is the area under $f$ over that range. Each named family has a fixed shape. The normal (Gaussian) family with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$ has the bell-shaped pdf below. The deciding rule: match the given formula to a family template and read off the parameters.

steps.title: Match the template
steps.body: The exponent is $-x^2/18$, so there is no shift: $\mu=0$. Compare $2\sigma^2$ with $18$: $\sigma^2=9$, $\sigma=3$. The constant in front is then $1/(3\sqrt{2\pi})$, which is exactly $1/(\sigma\sqrt{2\pi})$. Both parts of the template agree, so $X\sim N(0,9)$.

steps.title: Rule out the other families
steps.body: An exponential pdf is supported on $x\ge0$ only and has the form $\lambda e^{-\lambda x}$. A Poisson variable is discrete, so it has no pdf. A uniform pdf is constant on an interval. The given $f$ is defined on all real numbers, is not constant and is smooth, so only the normal fits. Answer: option B.

shortcut.body: Spot $e^{-x^2/\text{something}}$ over all reals and answer normal at once. Two seconds; no calculation is needed because every other option is either discrete, non-negative only, or flat.

traps.text: Exponential also decays, but it lives on $x\ge0$ and decays like $e^{-\lambda x}$, not $e^{-x^2}$.
Poisson is a discrete (counting) distribution and has a probability mass function, not a density over the reals.
Uniform means a constant density on an interval; this density changes with $x$.

recognize.clues: The density is defined for every real $x$, has $x^2$ inside a negative exponent and a front constant containing $\sqrt{2\pi}$. Those three features together mark the bell-curve family.
recognize.contrast: Exponential also uses $e^{-\text{something}}$ but with $x$ to the first power and only for $x\ge0$; the squared $x$ and the whole real line separate the two.

check.body: Integrate a bell curve with $\sigma=3$: the front constant $1/(3\sqrt{2\pi})$ is exactly what makes the total area 1, since $\int e^{-x^2/18}dx=3\sqrt{2\pi}$. A density that normalises with this constant and is symmetric about 0 is consistent with the identification.

questions.stem: Suppose an unbiased coin is tossed 6 times. Each coin toss is independent of all previous coin tosses. Let $E_1$ be the event that among the second, fourth, and sixth coin tosses, there are at least two heads. Let $E_2$ be the event that among the first, second, third, and fifth coin tosses, there are equal number of heads and tails. The conditional probability $P(E_1\mid E_2)$ is equal to ____________. (rounded off to one decimal place)

steps.title: Define the terms and the rule
steps.body: An event is a set of outcomes of the 6 tosses. The conditional probability $P(E_1\mid E_2)$ is the chance that $E_1$ happens when we already know $E_2$ happened. The rule: restrict attention to the outcomes inside $E_2$ and ask what fraction of them also lie in $E_1$.

steps.title: Count the outcomes of E2
steps.body: $E_2$ involves only tosses 1, 2, 3, 5. Equal heads and tails means exactly 2 heads among those 4 tosses: $\binom42=6$ patterns. Tosses 4 and 6 are free, so $E_2$ has $6\times4=24$ of the $64$ outcomes, and $P(E_2)=24/64=3/8$.

steps.title: Count what E1 needs, given E2
steps.body: Fix one of the 6 patterns of $E_2$. Toss 2 is part of that pattern. Toss 4 and toss 6 are free (4 combinations). $E_1$ needs at least 2 heads among tosses 2, 4, 6. Toss 2 is a head in $\binom31=3$ of the 6 patterns (choose where the other head goes among tosses 1, 3, 5), and a tail in the other 3.

steps.title: Add the two cases
steps.body: If toss 2 is a head (3 patterns): we need at least one head among tosses 4 and 6, which is $3$ of $4$ combinations. If toss 2 is a tail (3 patterns): we need both tosses 4 and 6 heads, which is $1$ of $4$. Favourable outcomes: $3\cdot3+3\cdot1=12$. So $P(E_1\cap E_2)=12/64$.

shortcut.body: Toss 2 is a head with probability $1/2$ given $E_2$ (by symmetry, 2 of 4 tosses are heads). Then the answer is $\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac34+\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac14=\tfrac12$. Takes under two minutes; it relies on tosses 4 and 6 being independent of $E_2$.

traps.text: 0.375 is $P(E_2)=24/64$, the denominator, not the conditional probability.

0.75 comes from assuming toss 2 is always a head inside $E_2$ (then $E_1$ needs one head from tosses 4 and 6, probability $3/4$); 0.1875 comes from stopping at the numerator $12/64$ without dividing by $P(E_2)$.

$E_1$ and $E_2$ turn out independent, because toss 2 is a head in exactly half of $E_2$'s patterns, so $P(E_1\mid E_2)=P(E_1)=4/8$. This is a coincidence of the setup, not a rule; compute the conditional to be sure.

recognize.clues: The wording asks for $P(E_1\mid E_2)$ with two events built from overlapping sets of fair coin tosses, so we shrink the sample space to $E_2$ and count inside it.
recognize.contrast: Independence would let us skip conditioning, but here the events share toss 2, so independence has to be checked rather than assumed.

check.body: Test independence directly. $E_1$ depends on tosses 2, 4, 6 and $E_2$ fixes exactly 2 heads among tosses 1, 2, 3, 5. Tosses 4 and 6 are free, and toss 2 is a head in 3 of the 6 patterns of $E_2$, which is a half, the same as its unconditional chance. So conditioning on $E_2$ leaves the law of tosses 2, 4, 6 unchanged and $P(E_1\mid E_2)=P(E_1)=4/8$, since 4 of the 8 patterns of three tosses have at least two heads. This matches the $12/24$ count.

questions.stem: An urn contains one red ball and one blue ball. At each step, a ball is picked uniformly at random from the urn, and this ball together with another ball of the same color is put back in the urn. The probability that there are equal number of red and blue balls after two steps is

solutionDiagram.alt: Probability tree of the urn after two steps. Red then blue and blue then red each reach 2 red 2 blue with probability 1/6.

steps.title: The process and the rule
steps.body: Each step draws one ball, then returns it plus one more ball of the same colour, so the urn grows by one ball and the colour just drawn becomes more likely next time. To combine steps we use the chain rule: the probability of a path is the product of the probability of each draw given what is in the urn at that moment. After two steps the urn holds 4 balls, so "equal" means 2 red and 2 blue.

steps.title: Which paths give 2 and 2
steps.body: Starting from 1R 1B, red twice gives 3R 1B and blue twice gives 1R 3B: unequal. To end at 2R 2B the two draws must differ: red then blue, or blue then red.

steps.title: Compute each path
steps.body: Red first: probability $1/2$, urn becomes 2R 1B. Then blue: probability $1/3$. Path probability $1/6$. Blue first: probability $1/2$, urn becomes 1R 2B, then red with probability $1/3$. Path probability $1/6$.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: The probability is $1/3$, option B.

shortcut.body: This urn is the Polya urn started at 1,1, for which every split after n steps is equally likely: after 2 steps the urn has 1, 2 or 3 red balls out of 4, and each of these 3 compositions has probability $1/3$. So 2R 2B is $1/3$. Safe only for the 1,1 start.

traps.text: Counting only one of the two paths (red then blue) and so getting $1/6$-type values, or using $(1/2)(1/2)$ and ignoring that the urn grows.
Assuming the draws stay 50-50 each step (ignoring the added ball), so that "different colours" has probability $1/2$.
Adding probabilities of the same-colour paths wrongly: $2/3$ is the probability that the two draws are the same colour, which gives unequal counts.

recognize.clues: A ball is drawn and returned with an extra ball of its colour, so each draw changes the odds of the next, and we want the chance of a final composition after two steps.
recognize.contrast: Drawing with plain replacement would keep every draw at $1/2$ and make the draws independent; the added ball here makes them dependent, so the chain rule is needed.

check.body: Sum all the leaves of the tree: the three possible final compositions (3 red, 2 each, 3 blue) must add to 1. Red twice is $\frac12\cdot\frac23=\frac13$ and blue twice is also $\frac13$, so the equal split must take the remaining $\frac13$.

questions.stem: Let $X$ be a random variable which takes values in the set $\{1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8\}$. Further, $\Pr(X=1)=\Pr(X=2)=\Pr(X=5)=\Pr(X=7)=\frac16$ and $\Pr(X=3)=\Pr(X=4)=\Pr(X=6)=\Pr(X=8)=\frac1{12}$. The expected value of $X$, denoted by $E[X]$, is equal to ___________. (rounded off to two decimal places)

steps.title: Definition
steps.body: A random variable $X$ assigns a number to each outcome. Its expected value (mean) is the probability-weighted average of its values: multiply each value by its probability and add. This is the single rule.

steps.title: Check the probabilities
steps.body: Four values have probability $1/6=2/12$ and four have $1/12$: total $4\cdot\frac{2}{12}+4\cdot\frac1{12}=\frac{12}{12}=1$, so the distribution is valid.

steps.title: Group by probability
steps.body: Values with probability $1/6$: $1+2+5+7=15$. Values with probability $1/12$: $3+4+6+8=21$.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: $E[X]=4.25$, inside the key range 4.24 to 4.26.

shortcut.body: Factor the common probability: $\frac{1}{12}(2\cdot15+21)=\frac{51}{12}=4.25$. Under one minute.

traps.text: 4.5 is the plain average of 1..8, ignoring the unequal probabilities.
Forgetting the denominators and using $15/6+21/6=6$ treats the 1/12 group as 1/6.

recognize.clues: The stem gives a full table of values with unequal probabilities and asks for $E[X]$, which is the weighted-average definition applied directly.
recognize.contrast: The plain mean of the listed values ignores the weights and is correct only when all values are equally likely; here two probabilities differ.

check.body: Compare with the unweighted mean $4.5$. The heavier weights fall on $1,2,5,7$, which average $3.75$, below $4.5$, so the true mean should land below $4.5$. The value $4.25$ is. Also, the weights sum to $\frac{4}{6}+\frac{4}{12}=1$.

questions.stem: A quadratic polynomial $(x-\alpha)(x-\beta)$ over complex numbers is said to be square invariant if $(x-\alpha)(x-\beta)=(x-\alpha^2)(x-\beta^2)$. Suppose from the set of all square invariant quadratic polynomials we choose one at random. The probability that the roots of the chosen polynomial are equal is __________. (rounded off to one decimal place)

steps.title: What the condition says
steps.body: A polynomial is determined by its pair of roots (as a multiset, since order does not matter). Two factored quadratics are equal exactly when their root multisets are equal. So square invariant means $\{\alpha,\beta\}=\{\alpha^2,\beta^2\}$. We then count such polynomials and see how many have a repeated root. "Chosen at random" means each distinct polynomial is equally likely.

steps.title: Case 1: each root maps to itself
steps.body: $\alpha^2=\alpha$ and $\beta^2=\beta$ force $\alpha,\beta\in\{0,1\}$. Unordered pairs: $\{0,0\},\{0,1\},\{1,1\}$, giving $x^2$, $x(x-1)$, $(x-1)^2$.

steps.title: Case 2: roots swap
steps.body: $\alpha^2=\beta$ and $\beta^2=\alpha$ give $\alpha^4=\alpha$, so $\alpha=0$ or $\alpha^3=1$. The values $0$ and $1$ repeat Case 1. The new ones are $\alpha=\omega$, $\beta=\omega^2$ with $\omega$ a primitive cube root of unity, giving $x^2+x+1$.

steps.title: Count
steps.body: The distinct square invariant polynomials are $x^2$, $x(x-1)$, $(x-1)^2$ and $x^2+x+1$: four in all. Equal roots: $x^2$ and $(x-1)^2$. A short script over roots in $\{0,1,\omega,\omega^2\}$ confirms 4 polynomials and 2 with equal roots.

shortcut.body: Roots must satisfy $r^4=r$ if they swap or $r^2=r$ if fixed, so the only candidates are $0,1,\omega,\omega^2$. List the valid pairs (4) and count repeated ones (2). About three minutes; the risk is missing the swap pair.

traps.text: 0.67 comes from forgetting the swap pair $\{\omega,\omega^2\}$: 3 polynomials, 2 with equal roots, giving $2/3$.
Counting ordered pairs $(\alpha,\beta)$ instead of distinct polynomials changes the denominator: $x(x-1)$ and $x^2+x+1$ each count twice, giving $2/6=0.33$.

recognize.clues: The sample space is the set of all square invariant polynomials, which first has to be listed by solving a root condition, and then a fraction of them is counted.
recognize.contrast: This is counting distinct polynomials, not ordered root pairs; counting ordered pairs changes the denominator.

check.body: Substitute each listed polynomial back. For $x^2+x+1$ the roots are $\omega,\omega^2$ with $\omega^3=1$, and squaring gives $\omega^2,\omega^4=\omega$, the same pair. For $x(x-1)$ the roots $0,1$ square to $0,1$. So each polynomial in the list is square invariant.

questions.stem: The unit interval $(0,1)$ is divided at a point chosen uniformly distributed over $(0,1)$ in $\mathbb{R}$ into two disjoint subintervals. The expected length of the subinterval that contains $0.4$ is ___________. (rounded off to two decimal places)

solutionDiagram.alt: Two copies of the unit interval. For a cut U above 0.4 the piece holding 0.4 is from 0 to U; for U below 0.4 it is from U to 1.

steps.title: Terms and rule
steps.body: A point $U$ is uniform on $(0,1)$ when its density is $1$ on that interval, so $P(a<U<b)=b-a$. The expected value of a quantity $g(U)$ is $\int g(u)\,f(u)\,du$ with $f=1$. The length of the piece containing $0.4$ depends on which side of $0.4$ the cut falls, so we split the integral at $0.4$.

steps.title: Length in each case
steps.body: If $U>0.4$, the cut is to the right of $0.4$, so the piece holding $0.4$ is $(0,U)$ with length $U$. If $U<0.4$, the piece is $(U,1)$ with length $1-U$.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: The expected length is $0.74$, inside the key range 0.70 to 0.80. It exceeds $0.5$ because the piece containing a given point tends to be the longer one.

shortcut.body: General formula for a point $p$: $E=\tfrac12+p(1-p)=0.5+0.24=0.74$. Check: $p=0.4$ gives $0.24$. One minute once the formula is known.

traps.text: 0.5 assumes each piece has expected length 1/2, ignoring that we pick the piece containing 0.4, not a random piece.
0.4 or 0.6 come from using only one side of the split, or the position of the point instead of a length.

recognize.clues: The cut point is uniform on $(0,1)$ and we want an expected length, so we integrate a length function against a constant density, splitting where the piece changes.
recognize.contrast: Do not confuse this with the expected length of a randomly chosen piece, which is $1/2$; here the piece is chosen by containing a given point.

check.body: Test the formula at the midpoint: for $p=0.5$ the piece containing it is the longer one, of length $\max(U,1-U)$, whose mean is $2\int_{0.5}^1 u\,du=0.75$, and $\tfrac12+0.5\cdot0.5=0.75$. Moving the point from $0.5$ to $0.4$ shortens the expected piece slightly, so a value just below $0.75$, namely $0.74$, is right.

questions.stem: A box contains 5 coins: 4 regular coins and 1 fake coin. When a regular coin is tossed, the probability $P(head)=0.5$ and for a fake coin, $P(head)=1$. You pick a coin at random and toss it twice, and get two heads. The probability that the coin you have chosen is the fake coin is _______. (rounded off to two decimal places)

steps.title: Bayes rule in words
steps.body: We observed an outcome (two heads) and want the probability of a cause (the coin is fake). Bayes rule weighs each cause by how likely it was beforehand (prior) times how likely it makes the observation (likelihood), then divides by the total.

steps.title: Fill in the numbers
steps.body: $P(F)=1/5$, $P(R)=4/5$. A fake coin gives two heads with probability $1$; a regular coin with probability $0.5\cdot0.5=1/4$.

steps.title: Compute
steps.body: Numerator: $1\cdot\frac15=\frac15$. Other term: $\frac14\cdot\frac45=\frac15$.

shortcut.body: Think in counts: of 20 equally likely coin-and-toss outcomes weighted, the fake gives weight 4 of HH and the four regular coins together give weight 4. Equal weights give 1/2. Under one minute.

traps.text: 0.2 is the prior $1/5$, ignoring the evidence.
0.33 comes from using one toss, or from forgetting to square the regular-coin likelihood: $\frac{1/5}{1/5+2/5}=1/3$. 0.25 is the likelihood $P(HH\mid R)$ read off as if it were the posterior.

recognize.clues: A coin is picked blindly from a mixed box, then evidence (two heads) is observed, and the question asks which type the coin was. Reasoning backward from the observation to the source marks Bayes.
recognize.contrast: Total probability would give the chance of two heads overall; Bayes goes one step further and divides the fake coin's share by that total.

check.body: Natural frequencies: picture 1000 draws. About 200 are the fake coin and all 200 show two heads. About 800 are regular coins and a quarter of them, 200, show two heads. So 400 draws show two heads and 200 of them are fake: $200/400=0.5$.

questions.stem: Suppose a 5-bit message is transmitted from a source to a destination through a noisy channel. The probability that a bit of the message gets flipped during transmission is 0.01. Flipping of each bit is independent of one another. The probability that the message is delivered error-free to the destination is ______ . (rounded off to three decimal places)

steps.title: Independence rule
steps.body: Two events are independent when knowing one tells nothing about the other; then the probability that all happen is the product of their individual probabilities. Here each bit is flipped independently with probability $0.01$, so each bit arrives intact with probability $0.99$. "Error-free" means all 5 bits arrive intact (a Binomial with zero flips).

shortcut.body: $(1-x)^5\approx1-5x=0.95$ gives 0.95, and the second-order correction $+10x^2=0.001$ gives $0.951$. Under a minute.

traps.text: 0.95 comes from the first-order approximation $1-5(0.01)$; the key range needs three decimals.
0.99 uses one bit instead of five; 0.049 is $1-0.951$, the probability of at least one error.

questions.stem: Consider a probability distribution given by the density function $P(x)$. $$P(x)=\begin{cases}Cx^2,&\text{for }1\le x\le4\\0,&\text{for }x<1\text{ or }x>4\end{cases}$$ The probability that $x$ lies between 2 and 3, i.e., $P(2\le x\le3)$ is __________. (rounded off to three decimal places)

steps.title: What a density must satisfy
steps.body: A probability density function is non-negative and the total area under it is $1$ (the chance that $x$ takes some value). The probability of a range is the area under the density over that range. Since $C$ is unknown, the total-area rule fixes it first.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: Rounded to three decimals this is $0.302$, inside the key range 0.300 to 0.302.

shortcut.body: The constant cancels in the ratio of cubes: $\frac{3^3-2^3}{4^3-1^3}=\frac{19}{63}=0.302$. Under a minute.

traps.text: 0.333 treats the density as uniform on $[1,4]$, giving $(3-2)/(4-1)$ and ignoring the $x^2$ weighting.
Skipping normalisation: $\int_2^3 x^2 dx=6.33$ is not a probability.

recognize.clues: A named function $P(x)$ with an unknown constant $C$, a stated support $[1,4]$ and a request for the probability of a sub-interval: a continuous density that must be normalised first.
recognize.contrast: A uniform density also has a constant height on its support, but here the weight is $x^2$, so intervals of equal length do not carry equal probability and a length ratio gives the wrong value.

check.body: Split the support into $[1,2]$, $[2,3]$ and $[3,4]$. Their raw areas are proportional to $2^3-1^3$, $3^3-2^3$ and $4^3-3^3$, which are $7$, $19$ and $37$. These add up to the whole-support total of $63$, so the three probabilities sum to 1 and the middle one is the share $19/63$.

questions.stem: When six unbiased dice are rolled simultaneously, the probability of getting all distinct numbers (i.e., 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6) is

steps.title: Equally likely outcomes
steps.body: Each die has 6 faces, and the six dice are distinguishable (die 1, die 2, ...), so a roll is an ordered 6-tuple. There are $6^6=46656$ equally likely tuples. The rule: probability equals favourable tuples divided by total tuples.

steps.title: Favourable outcomes
steps.body: All faces distinct means the tuple is a permutation of $1,\dots,6$: $6!=720$ of them.

shortcut.body: Chain it: $\frac66\cdot\frac56\cdot\frac46\cdot\frac36\cdot\frac26\cdot\frac16=\frac{720}{46656}$. Then test by cancelling: $720=144\cdot5$.

traps.text: $1/324$ comes from reducing $720/46656$ by dividing the numerator by $720$ but the denominator by only $144$; the same fraction must be divided top and bottom by the same number.
$7/324$ keeps the right denominator with a wrong numerator: it would need $1008$ favourable tuples, more than the $6!=720$ permutations that exist.
$11/324$ would need $1584$ favourable tuples, more than the $720$ permutations; check any reduction by decimals: $720/46656\approx0.0154$ and $5/324\approx0.0154$.

recognize.clues: Six dice rolled together and a request that all faces differ: a finite sample space of equally likely ordered outcomes, so the method is favourable count over total count.
recognize.contrast: Binomial or geometric thinking fits repeated trials with one success chance. Here the event is a joint pattern across all six dice, so counting arrangements is simpler than tracking trials one at a time.

check.body: Reciprocal route: $46656/720=64.8$ and $324/5=64.8$, so the probability is $1/64.8\approx0.0154$. This matches $5/324$, while $1/324\approx0.0031$, $7/324\approx0.0216$ and $11/324\approx0.0340$ do not.

questions.stem: Let $x$ and $y$ be random variables, not necessarily independent, that take real values in the interval $[0,1]$. Let $z=xy$ and let the mean values of $x,y,z$ be $\bar x,\bar y,\bar z$, respectively. Which one of the following statements is TRUE?

steps.title: Terms
steps.body: The mean $\bar x=E[x]$ is the probability-weighted average. Two facts decide the question: (1) expectation preserves inequalities, so if $u\le v$ always then $E[u]\le E[v]$; (2) $E[xy]=E[x]E[y]$ holds only when $x,y$ are independent (more precisely uncorrelated), and the question says they need not be.

steps.title: Option D follows
steps.body: Because $y\in[0,1]$ and $x\ge0$, we have $xy\le x$ in every outcome. Taking expectations, $\bar z\le\bar x$.
steps.tex: 0\le y\le1,\ x\ge0\Rightarrow xy\le x\Rightarrow \bar z\le\bar x

steps.title: Options A, B, C fail on counterexamples
steps.body: Let $x=y$ be 0 or 1 with probability $1/2$ each. Then $z=x$, $\bar z=0.5$ while $\bar x\bar y=0.25$: so $\bar z>\bar x\bar y$, killing A and B. Let $y=1-x$. Then $z=0$, $\bar z=0<0.25$: so C fails. Only D holds in every case.

shortcut.body: Test two extreme dependent pairs, $y=x$ and $y=1-x$ with $x\in\{0,1\}$: they break A, B and C immediately, leaving D. About two minutes.

traps.text: Assuming $E[xy]=E[x]E[y]$, which needs independence.
Thinking a product of numbers in $[0,1]$ is smaller, so its mean is smaller than the product of means; true for $y=1-x$ but false for $y=x$.
Using positive correlation as if it always held; negative correlation reverses it.

recognize.clues: Variables described as not necessarily independent, with values in $[0,1]$, and statements comparing the mean of $xy$ with other means: a question about which expectation rules survive without independence.
recognize.contrast: Independence gives $E[xy]=E[x]E[y]$ and is the look-alike. The phrase "not necessarily independent" removes it, leaving only inequalities that hold in every single outcome.

check.body: Test the surviving inequality $\bar z\le\bar x$ at its boundaries. If $y=1$ always then $z=x$ and the two means are equal; if $y=0$ always then $\bar z=0\le\bar x$. Both ends respect it, and no choice of $y$ in $[0,1]$ can push $z$ above $x$.

questions.stem: Consider a permutation sampled uniformly at random from the set of all permutations of $\{1,2,3,\cdots,n\}$ for some $n\ge4$. Let $X$ be the event that 1 occurs before 2 in the permutation, and $Y$ the event that 3 occurs before 4. Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
options: The events $X$ and $Y$ are mutually exclusive
Event $X$ is more likely than event $Y$

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: Mutually exclusive: both cannot happen together ($P(X\cap Y)=0$). Independent: $P(X\cap Y)=P(X)P(Y)$. A uniformly random permutation is symmetric: every ordering of any chosen elements is equally likely.

steps.title: Compute P(X), P(Y)
steps.body: Looking only at the relative order of 1 and 2, the two orders are equally likely, so $P(X)=1/2$. Likewise $P(Y)=1/2$. So D is false.

steps.title: Compute P(X and Y)
steps.body: Consider the relative order of the four elements 1, 2, 3, 4: all $4!=24$ orders are equally likely. Orders with 1 before 2 and 3 before 4: choose positions for the pair $\{1,2\}$ in order and $\{3,4\}$ in order: $\frac{4!}{2\cdot2}=6$. So $P(X\cap Y)=6/24=1/4=P(X)P(Y)$.

steps.title: Conclude
steps.body: $X$ and $Y$ are independent, option B. They can occur together (A false) and both can fail (2 before 1 and 4 before 3), so C is false.

shortcut.body: Disjoint pairs of elements are ordered independently in a uniform permutation, and each pair order is a fair coin. Pick B in seconds. Unsafe if the pairs shared an element (e.g. 1<2 and 2<3).

traps.text: Both events can occur: the permutation 1 2 3 4 does it.
The permutation 2 1 4 3 makes both fail.
Both probabilities are exactly $1/2$ by symmetry; no pair is favoured.

recognize.clues: Two events defined on disjoint pairs of elements of one random permutation, with options naming mutual exclusion, independence, certainty and likelihood: the vocabulary of the product test.
recognize.contrast: Mutually exclusive is often confused with independent. Exclusive events have an empty overlap, while independent events have an overlap equal to the product, so exclusive events of positive probability are never independent.

check.body: Second route by conditioning: given that $1$ precedes $2$, the relative order of $3$ and $4$ is still equally likely either way, because swapping the labels $3$ and $4$ maps permutations to permutations and keeps $1$ before $2$. So $P(Y\mid X)=P(Y)$, the conditional form of independence.

questions.stem: Let $A$ and $B$ be two events in a probability space with $P(A)=0.3$, $P(B)=0.5$, and $P(A\cap B)=0.1$. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
options: The two events $A$ and $B$ are independent
$P(A\cap B^c)=0.2$, where $B^c$ is the complement of the event $B$
$P(A^c\cap B^c)=0.4$, where $A^c$ and $B^c$ are the complements of the events $A$ and $B$, respectively

solutionDiagram.alt: Venn diagram of A and B with region probabilities: A only 0.2, both 0.1, B only 0.4, outside both 0.3.

steps.title: Rules used
steps.body: Independent means $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$. Union: $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$. The part of $A$ outside $B$ is $P(A\cap B^c)=P(A)-P(A\cap B)$. De Morgan: $A^c\cap B^c$ is the complement of $A\cup B$. Dividing the plane into four regions makes all of these a subtraction.

steps.title: Check each statement
steps.body: A: $P(A)P(B)=0.15\ne0.1$, false. B: $0.3+0.5-0.1=0.7$, true. C: $0.2$, true. D: $P(A^c\cap B^c)=1-0.7=0.3\ne0.4$, false. Answer: B and C.
steps.tex: P(A\cup B)=0.7,\ P(A\cap B^c)=0.2,\ P(A^c\cap B^c)=0.3

shortcut.body: Draw the four regions (0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.3) and read each statement off. Under a minute.

traps.text: Calling A true: $P(A)P(B)=0.15$ is not $0.1$, so the events are dependent.
Calling D true: $0.4$ is the "B only" region, not the region outside both. The outside region is $1-0.7=0.3$.
Leaving out C by treating $P(A\cap B^c)$ as $P(A)P(B^c)=0.15$, which holds only under independence.

recognize.clues: Three probabilities are given, $P(A)$, $P(B)$ and $P(A\cap B)$, and each option asks for another set expression: independence itself, a union, a difference or the complement of a union.
recognize.contrast: Total probability and Bayes need a partition with conditional probabilities. No conditional is given here, so the four-region split is the whole method.

check.body: Get the "neither" region by a different route: $P(A^c\cap B^c)=P(B^c)-P(A\cap B^c)=0.5-0.2=0.3$, which agrees with $1-P(A\cup B)=0.3$. So statement D (0.4) fails, and $P(A\cup B)=P(B)+P(A\cap B^c)=0.5+0.2=0.7$ confirms statement B.

solutionDiagram.alt: The four equally likely outcomes of two coin tosses with events A, B and C marked, and a table comparing P(X and Y) with P(X)P(Y) for each pair: A and B fail, A and C fail, B and C pass.

steps.title: Events, probability and independence
steps.body: A random experiment has a sample space, the list of all its outcomes. Two fair coins give four equally likely outcomes HH, HT, TH, TT, each with probability $\frac14$. An event is a set of outcomes, and its probability is the number of outcomes in it divided by 4. Two events are independent when knowing that one happened does not change the chance of the other. The single rule that decides it is the product test: $X$ and $Y$ are independent exactly when $\Pr(X\cap Y)=\Pr(X)\Pr(Y)$. Conditional probability is $\Pr(X\mid Y)=\Pr(X\cap Y)/\Pr(Y)$, so for $\Pr(Y)>0$ the product test says the same thing as $\Pr(X\mid Y)=\Pr(X)$.

steps.title: Write the three events as sets
steps.body: $A=\{HH\}$, $B=\{HH,HT\}$ (first throw is HEAD) and $C=\{HH,TH\}$ (second throw is HEAD). So $\Pr(A)=\frac14$ and $\Pr(B)=\Pr(C)=\frac24=\frac12$. Every pairwise intersection is the single outcome HH: $A\cap B=A\cap C=B\cap C=\{HH\}$, probability $\frac14$ each.

steps.title: Apply the product test to each pair
steps.body: $A,B$: $\Pr(A\cap B)=\frac14$ but $\Pr(A)\Pr(B)=\frac14\cdot\frac12=\frac18$. They differ, so $A$ and $B$ are not independent; option A is false. $A,C$ is the same computation, so option B is false. $B,C$: $\Pr(B)\Pr(C)=\frac12\cdot\frac12=\frac14=\Pr(B\cap C)$, so $B$ and $C$ are independent; option C is true.

steps.title: Check option D and answer
steps.body: $\Pr(B\mid C)=\Pr(B\cap C)/\Pr(C)=\frac{1/4}{1/2}=\frac12=\Pr(B)$, so option D is true. It is the conditional form of the independence in option C, so the two always stand or fall together. Answer: C and D, the key $C;D$.

shortcut.body: The two tosses are separate coins, so the first-throw event $B$ and second-throw event $C$ are independent at once, and option D is the same statement in conditional form: C and D are true together. $A$ sits inside $B$ with $\Pr(A)=\frac14<\Pr(B)=\frac12$, so $\Pr(A\mid B)=\frac12\ne\Pr(A)$: an event strictly inside another, neither impossible nor certain, is never independent of it. About one minute.

traps.text: HEAD on both throws sounds unrelated to HEAD on the first throw, but $A$ is a subset of $B$: $\Pr(A\mid B)=\frac12$ while $\Pr(A)=\frac14$, so knowing $B$ doubles the chance of $A$.
Same slip with the second throw: $\Pr(A\cap C)=\frac14\ne\frac18=\Pr(A)\Pr(C)$. Two throws being independent does not make an event built from both throws independent of one throw.
Leaving D out because it looks like a different kind of statement. $\Pr(B\mid C)=\Pr(B)$ is the definition of independence rewritten, so it must be true whenever C is.

recognize.clues: Two fair coins give a small equally likely sample space, and the options mix pairwise independence tests with a conditional-probability equation.
recognize.contrast: Mutually exclusive events cannot occur together. These events overlap in the outcome HH, and overlap alone does not decide independence, so only the product test can settle each pair.

check.body: Check one pair from the physical setup. Event $B$ depends only on the first coin and $C$ only on the second, and separate fair coins do not influence each other, so $\Pr(B\cap C)$ must factor. The count-based product test must agree with that, and it does only for this pair.

questions.stem: For a given biased coin, the probability that the outcome of a toss is a head is $0.4$. This coin is tossed 1,000 times. Let $X$ denote the random variable whose value is the number of times that head appeared in these 1,000 tosses. The standard deviation of $X$ (rounded to 2 decimal places) is ______.

steps.title: The binomial distribution and its spread
steps.body: Toss a coin $n$ times, each toss independent, with head probability $p$. The number of heads $X$ is binomial. The mean is the average value of $X$. The variance is the average squared distance from the mean, and the standard deviation is its square root, which has the same unit as $X$. The rule: $X$ is a sum of $n$ independent 0-or-1 tosses, variances of independent variables add, and one toss has variance $p(1-p)$, so $\mathrm{Var}(X)=np(1-p)$.

steps.title: Variance of one toss
steps.body: Let $X_i=1$ if toss $i$ is a head, else 0. Then $E[X_i]=p=0.4$ and $E[X_i^2]=p$ because $X_i^2=X_i$. So $\mathrm{Var}(X_i)=p-p^2=p(1-p)=0.4\times0.6=0.24$.

steps.title: Add over 1,000 tosses and take the root
steps.body: The tosses are independent, so $\mathrm{Var}(X)=1000\times0.24=240$ and $\sigma=\sqrt{240}=15.4919\ldots\approx15.49$. This lies inside the key range 15.00 to 16.00.

shortcut.body: $\sqrt{240}$ lies between $15$ ($15^2=225$) and $16$ ($16^2=256$), and the official key accepts any value from 15.00 to 16.00, so there is no need to compute the digits. About 30 seconds.

traps.text: Giving $240$ (the variance) or $400$ (the mean $np$): the question asks for the standard deviation, so the square root is the last step.
Using $\sqrt{np}=\sqrt{400}=20$. That is the Poisson spread, where variance equals mean; for a binomial the factor $(1-p)$ shrinks the variance.
Using $p$ twice, $\sqrt{1000\times0.4\times0.4}=12.65$, instead of $p(1-p)$ with $1-p=0.6$.

recognize.clues: A fixed number of independent tosses (1,000), one head probability ($0.4$), and a variable that counts heads.
recognize.contrast: Geometric counts tosses until the first head, but here the number of tosses is fixed and the heads vary, so it is binomial. Poisson has variance equal to its mean, which fails here.

check.body: Boundary comparison: a fair coin gives the largest spread for 1,000 tosses, $\sqrt{1000\times0.25}\approx15.81$. A bias of $0.4$ makes the variance factor $0.24$, slightly below $0.25$, so the result must be slightly below $15.81$. At $p=0$ or $p=1$ the spread is zero, as it should be.

questions.stem: In an examination, a student can choose the order in which two questions (QuesA and QuesB) must be attempted. If the first question is answered wrong, the student gets zero marks. If the first question is answered correctly and the second question is not answered correctly, the student gets the marks only for the first question. If both the questions are answered correctly, the student gets the sum of the marks of the two questions. The following table shows the probability of correctly answering a question and the marks of the question respectively. Assuming that the student always wants to maximize her expected marks in the examination, in which order should she attempt the questions and what is the expected marks for that order (assume that the questions are independent)?

solutionDiagram.alt: Two decision trees side by side. Attempting QuesA first: wrong 0.2 gives 0 marks, right then wrong gives 10, right then right gives 30, so expected marks 0.8 times (10 plus 0.5 times 20) equals 16. Attempting QuesB first gives 14.

options: First QuesA and then QuesB. Expected marks 14.
First QuesB and then QuesA. Expected marks 14.
First QuesB and then QuesA. Expected marks 22.
First QuesA and then QuesB. Expected marks 16.

steps.title: Expected marks and what the order changes
steps.body: The expected value of a quantity is the probability-weighted average of its possible values. Here the marks come in stages: the second question counts only if the first is answered correctly. With independent questions, the chance that both are right is the product of the two chances. So if the first question has probability $p_1$ and marks $m_1$, the second $p_2$ and $m_2$, the expected marks are $p_1\,(m_1+p_2m_2)$: with probability $p_1$ she keeps $m_1$, and within that case she gains $m_2$ with probability $p_2$.

steps.title: Order QuesA then QuesB
steps.body: $p_1=0.8$, $m_1=10$, $p_2=0.5$, $m_2=20$. Outcomes: first wrong, probability $0.2$, marks $0$; first right and second wrong, $0.8\times0.5=0.4$, marks $10$; both right, $0.4$, marks $30$. So $E=0.4\times10+0.4\times30=4+12=16$.

steps.title: Order QuesB then QuesA
steps.body: Now $p_1=0.5$, $m_1=20$, $p_2=0.8$, $m_2=10$. Outcomes: first wrong, $0.5$, marks $0$; first right and second wrong, $0.5\times0.2=0.1$, marks $20$; both right, $0.5\times0.8=0.4$, marks $30$. So $E=0.1\times20+0.4\times30=2+12=14$.

steps.title: Choose the better order
steps.body: $16>14$, so she should attempt QuesA first and then QuesB, with expected marks $16$. That is option D. The harder question is not the one to put first: it is more likely to be answered wrong, which would throw away the easy question's marks.

shortcut.body: Compare the two orders without computing both totals. The difference is $E_{AB}-E_{BA}=p_Am_A(1-p_B)-p_Bm_B(1-p_A)$. Here $0.8\times10\times0.5=4$ beats $0.5\times20\times0.2=2$, so QuesA goes first. Only options A and D put QuesA first, and $0.8\times(10+10)=16$ picks D. About two minutes.

traps.text: Right order, wrong number: $14$ is the expected marks of the opposite order, QuesB then QuesA.
Putting the 20-mark question first because it carries more marks. Its success chance is only $0.5$, so half the time the easy 10 marks are never collected.
$22$ exceeds both orders' values ($16$ and $14$); neither order reaches it, because the second question counts only after the first is correct.

recognize.clues: Marks that depend on a sequence of answers, a table of probabilities and marks for each question, and the wish to maximise expected marks over the choice of order.
recognize.contrast: Total probability would split on a hidden cause; here the split is on what happens in sequence and every branch has known marks, so a plain weighted average over branches is the tool.

check.body: Count marks per question instead of per outcome. QuesA's marks are earned whenever A is answered right and, if A is first, that is probability $0.8$. QuesB's marks need B right and A right as well, probability $0.8\times0.5=0.4$. So $E_{AB}=10(0.8)+20(0.4)=16$. For the other order, $E_{BA}=20(0.5)+10(0.4)=14$. This second route gives the same pair of totals.

questions.stem: A bag has $r$ red balls and $b$ black balls. All balls are identical except for their colours. In a trial, a ball is randomly drawn from the bag, its colour is noted and the ball is placed back into the bag along with another ball of the same colour. Note that the number of balls in the bag will increase by one, after the trial. A sequence of four such trials is conducted. Which one of the following choices gives the probability of drawing a red ball in the fourth trial?

steps.title: The process and the tools
steps.body: Each trial draws one ball at random, then returns it together with one more ball of the same colour. So the bag grows by one ball per trial, and whichever colour was drawn becomes more likely next time. Probability at one trial depends on the history, so we use two tools. Total probability: split on what happened earlier, $\Pr(R)=\sum \Pr(R\mid\text{history})\Pr(\text{history})$. The multiplication rule: the chance of a sequence of draws is the product of the chance of each draw given the draws before it. Let $R_k$ be the event that trial $k$ is red.

steps.title: Second trial, as a warm-up
steps.body: After a first red draw the bag holds $r+1$ red and $b$ black out of $r+b+1$; after a first black draw it holds $r$ red out of $r+b+1$. By total probability the second trial is red with probability the expression below, which equals the first trial's $\frac{r}{r+b}$.

steps.title: Why the fourth trial is the same
steps.body: Take any sequence of four colours with $k$ reds. Its probability is a product of four fractions. The denominators are always $(r+b)(r+b+1)(r+b+2)(r+b+3)$, whatever the colours. The numerators are $r,r+1,\dots,r+k-1$ for the reds and $b,b+1,\dots,b+3-k$ for the blacks, in the order they appear. Those two lists do not depend on the order of the colours. So a sequence's probability depends only on how many reds it has, not on where they sit.

steps.title: Swap trial 1 and trial 4
steps.body: Swapping the colours of trial 1 and trial 4 in a sequence gives another sequence with the same number of reds, hence the same probability. This swap pairs up the sequences with a red fourth draw and the sequences with a red first draw, so $\Pr(R_4)=\Pr(R_1)=\frac{r}{r+b}$. That is option A. Numerical check with $r=2$, $b=3$: exact enumeration gives $\frac25$; options B, C, D give $\frac14$, $\frac58$, $\frac1{14}$.

shortcut.body: Take the smallest case $r=b=1$. Red and black play identical roles, so any trial is red with probability exactly $\frac12$. Option A gives $\frac12$; B gives $\frac15$, C gives $\frac45$, D gives $\frac15$. Only A survives. Unsafe in general for questions without symmetry, but here it kills three options in half a minute.

traps.text: $\frac{r}{r+b+3}$ divides by the final size of the bag but keeps the original $r$ reds. It forgets that reds are added during the first three trials, and reds appear in the bag only when red balls were drawn.
$\frac{r+3}{r+b+3}$ assumes the first three draws were all red. That is one possible history, not the average over all histories.
The product is the probability that all four draws are red, not that the fourth is red. For $r=2$, $b=3$ it is $\frac1{14}$, far below $\frac25$.

recognize.clues: A draw whose result changes the contents of the bag, and a question about a later draw in the sequence rather than the first, so the earlier draws must be summed over.
recognize.contrast: This is not the product of four draws: that would be the chance of red on every trial. Asking about one trial alone means summing over all histories of the others.

check.body: Boundary cases. With $b=0$ every ball is red and every trial must give probability $1$; with $r=0$ it must give $0$. Option A gives $\frac{r}{r}=1$ and $0$. Option B gives $\frac{r}{r+3}\ne1$ at $b=0$, and option C gives $\frac{3}{b+3}\ne0$ at $r=0$. Option D is the chance of four reds in a row; red on trial 4 also happens after histories containing a black ball, which have positive probability when $b>0$, so D is strictly smaller than the wanted value and cannot equal it. Only A is left.

questions.stem: The lifetime of a component of a certain type is a random variable whose probability density function is exponentially distributed with parameter $2$. For a randomly picked component of this type, the probability that its lifetime exceeds the expected lifetime (rounded to 2 decimal places) is ______.

solutionDiagram.alt: Graph of the exponential density 2 e to the minus 2x with the mean 0.5 marked and the area to its right shaded, which equals e to the minus 1, about 0.37.

steps.title: The exponential distribution
steps.body: A lifetime $X$ is exponential with rate $\lambda>0$ when its density is $f(x)=\lambda e^{-\lambda x}$ for $x\ge0$. Two facts decide this question. The expected lifetime (mean) is $E[X]=1/\lambda$. The chance of surviving beyond time $t$ is the area under the density to the right of $t$: $\Pr(X>t)=e^{-\lambda t}$. \"Parameter $2$\" is the rate, $\lambda=2$.

steps.title: Expected lifetime
steps.body: With $\lambda=2$: $E[X]=\frac12$. The question asks for $\Pr\!\left(X>\frac12\right)$.

steps.title: Survival beyond the mean
steps.body: $\Pr(X>\tfrac12)=e^{-2\cdot\frac12}=e^{-1}=0.3679\approx0.37$, inside the key range 0.35 to 0.39. If \"parameter 2\" were read as the mean instead, then $\lambda=\frac12$ and $t=2$, so $\lambda t=1$ again. The rate cancels, and the answer is the same.

shortcut.body: For any exponential variable the chance of exceeding its own mean is $e^{-1}\approx 0.368$, whatever the rate. Remember $e\approx2.72$, so $1/e\approx0.37$. Ten seconds. The key accepts 0.35 to 0.39.

traps.text: $0.50$: the median is the point with probability $\frac12$ on each side, but for an exponential the median ($\ln2/\lambda$) is below the mean, so the chance of exceeding the mean is less than $\frac12$.
$0.14$: that is $e^{-2}$, which uses $t=1$ instead of $t=\frac12$ (the mean). The exponent is rate times time, $2\times\frac12=1$.
$0.63$: that is $1-e^{-1}$, the probability that the lifetime is below the mean. The question asks for exceeding it.

recognize.clues: The phrase lifetime with an exponentially distributed density and a parameter, together with a comparison against the expected lifetime itself.
recognize.contrast: A normal variable would have its mean equal to its median, giving one half above the mean. The exponential is skewed, so the chance above its mean is not one half.

check.body: The exponential has a median of $\frac{\ln2}{\lambda}=0.347$ here, below the mean $0.5$. Exactly half the probability lies beyond the median, so the chance of exceeding the larger value $0.5$ must be under $0.5$. The value $e^{-1}=0.368$ fits that ordering, while $0.5$ and $0.63$ do not.

variation.stem: The lifetime of a device is exponentially distributed with rate parameter $5$. For a randomly picked device, what is the probability that its lifetime exceeds twice the expected lifetime? Give the answer rounded to 2 decimal places.
variation.explanation: The mean is $\frac15$, so twice the mean is $\frac25$. The tail is $\Pr(X>\tfrac25)=e^{-5\times 2/5}=e^{-2}=0.1353\approx0.14$. The rate cancels, so any exponential gives $e^{-2}$ for twice its mean.

questions.stem: Consider the two statements. $S_1$: There exist random variables $X$ and $Y$ such that $\left(\mathbb{E}\big[(X-\mathbb{E}(X))(Y-\mathbb{E}(Y))\big]\right)^2>\mathrm{Var}[X]\,\mathrm{Var}[Y]$. $S_2$: For all random variables $X$ and $Y$, $\mathrm{Cov}[X,Y]=\mathbb{E}\big[\,|X-\mathbb{E}[X]|\,|Y-\mathbb{E}[Y]|\,\big]$. Which one of the following choices is correct?

steps.title: Definitions and the rule
steps.body: Let $U=X-E[X]$ and $V=Y-E[Y]$, the deviations from the means. The variance is $\mathrm{Var}[X]=E[U^2]$, and the covariance is $\mathrm{Cov}[X,Y]=E[UV]$. It is positive when the deviations tend to have the same sign and negative when they tend to have opposite signs. The statement $S_1$ says the squared covariance can beat the product of the variances. The rule that decides it is the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality: always $\mathrm{Cov}[X,Y]^2\le\mathrm{Var}[X]\,\mathrm{Var}[Y]$, which is the reason a correlation coefficient never leaves $[-1,1]$.

steps.title: S1 is false: proof of the inequality
steps.body: For every real $t$, the square $(U-tV)^2$ is never negative, so its expectation is never negative: $0\le E[U^2]-2t\,E[UV]+t^2E[V^2]$. A quadratic in $t$ that never goes below zero has discriminant at most zero. That gives $4E[UV]^2-4E[U^2]E[V^2]\le0$, which is the inequality above. (If $E[V^2]=0$ then $V=0$ with probability 1 and both sides are 0.) So no pair of variables makes the left side strictly larger; $S_1$ is false.

steps.title: S2 is false: a counterexample
steps.body: Let $X$ be $+1$ or $-1$ with probability $\frac12$ each, and $Y=-X$. Both means are $0$, so $U=X$ and $V=-X$. Then $\mathrm{Cov}[X,Y]=E[-X^2]=-1$, but $E[|X||Y|]=E[1]=1$. Since $-1\ne1$, the claim fails. In general $E[|U||V|]\ge0$ always, so $S_2$ would force every covariance to be non-negative, which is false.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: Both $S_1$ and $S_2$ are false, option D.

shortcut.body: Right side of $S_2$ is the average of a non-negative quantity, so it can never be negative, yet covariance can be (two variables moving in opposite directions): $S_2$ false. $S_1$ would put correlation outside $[-1,1]$: false. Both false, D, in about one minute.

traps.text: Believing both: $S_2$ looks like a harmless rewrite of the covariance formula, but absolute values destroy the sign, and the sign is exactly what covariance records.
Taking $S_1$ as true would mean a correlation larger than 1 exists. Dropping the intuition that $|\rho|\le1$ makes the squared covariance look unconstrained.
Taking $S_2$ as true and $S_1$ as false is right about $S_1$ only. $S_2$ holds when both deviations always share a sign, as when $Y=X$, but that is a special case, not \"for all\".

recognize.clues: Two claims about all random variables that compare a squared covariance with a product of variances and rewrite covariance with absolute values.
recognize.contrast: Correlation coefficient bounds follow from the inequality between covariance and variances; the absolute-value rewrite is a different quantity, because covariance keeps the sign of the deviations.

check.body: For $S_1$, take the extreme case $Y=2X$. Then $\mathrm{Cov}[X,Y]=2\mathrm{Var}[X]$, so its square is $4\mathrm{Var}[X]^2$, and $\mathrm{Var}[X]\mathrm{Var}[Y]=4\mathrm{Var}[X]^2$ too: the two sides are equal, the most that perfect dependence can reach, not larger. For $S_2$, $Y=-X$ with $X=\pm1$ gives a covariance of $-1$ against $1$.

questions.stem: A sender ($S$) transmits a signal, which can be one of the two kinds: $H$ and $L$ with probabilities $0.1$ and $0.9$ respectively, to a receiver ($R$). In the graph below, the weight of edge $(u,v)$ is the probability of receiving $v$ when $u$ is transmitted, where $u,v\in\{H,L\}$. For example, the probability that the received signal is $L$ given the transmitted signal was $H$, is $0.7$. If the received signal is $H$, the probability that the transmitted signal was $H$ (rounded to 2 decimal places) is ______.
questions.figure: A bipartite graph with S on the left and R on the right, each with two nodes H and L. The sender sends H with probability 0.1 and L with probability 0.9. Edges and weights: H to H 0.3, H to L 0.7, L to H 0.8, L to L 0.2.

diagram.alt: Bipartite graph: sender nodes H (prior 0.1) and L (prior 0.9) on the left, receiver nodes H and L on the right, with edge weights H to H 0.3, H to L 0.7, L to H 0.8, L to L 0.2.

solutionDiagram.alt: Probability tree: sent H with 0.1 then received H with 0.3 gives 0.03; sent L with 0.9 then received H with 0.8 gives 0.72; the posterior is 0.03 divided by 0.75, which is 0.04.

steps.title: The question reverses a conditional probability
steps.body: The graph gives the chance of what is received given what was sent, $\Pr(R\mid S)$. The question asks the reverse: given what was received, how likely was each sent signal, $\Pr(S\mid R)$. Bayes' rule converts one into the other. The prior $\Pr(S)$ is how often each signal is sent. The denominator is the total chance of receiving $H$, found by adding over both possible senders (total probability).

steps.title: Read the numbers off the graph
steps.body: Sent $H$ with probability $0.1$, sent $L$ with $0.9$. From $H$: received $H$ with $0.3$, received $L$ with $0.7$. From $L$: received $H$ with $0.8$ (the crossing edge), received $L$ with $0.2$. Each sender's two edges sum to 1, which confirms the labels: the stem fixes $H\to L=0.7$, so the other crossing edge $L\to H$ is $0.8$.

steps.title: Total probability of receiving H
steps.body: $H$ is received in two ways: sent $H$ and received $H$ ($0.1\times0.3=0.03$), or sent $L$ and received $H$ ($0.9\times0.8=0.72$). Adding, $\Pr(R{=}H)=0.75$.

steps.title: Posterior
steps.body: Only the 0.03 of the 0.75 came from a sent $H$: $\Pr(S{=}H\mid R{=}H)=\frac{0.03}{0.75}=0.04$. The common signal $L$ is mis-received as $H$ so often that a received $H$ is almost surely a sent $L$.

shortcut.body: Only two numbers matter, the two ways to receive $H$: $0.1\times0.3=0.03$ and $0.9\times0.8=0.72$. The answer is the first as a fraction of their sum, $\frac{0.03}{0.75}=\frac1{25}=0.04$. About 90 seconds.

traps.text: $0.3$ or $0.1$: reading an edge weight or the prior as the answer. Edge $H\to H$ is $\Pr(R{=}H\mid S{=}H)$, the wrong direction.
$0.03$: stopping at the joint probability. It must be divided by $\Pr(R{=}H)=0.75$.
$0.96$: this is $0.72/0.75$, the posterior of a sent $L$. It answers the complementary question.

recognize.clues: A channel diagram with edge weights as chances of receiving given sending, priors on the sent signals, and a question about the sent signal given what was received.
recognize.contrast: Plain conditional probability would read the edge weight directly; here the asked direction is opposite to the edge, so the prior and the total chance of the observation must enter.

check.body: Count in a population of $1000$ messages. About $100$ are sent as $H$ and $900$ as $L$. Of these, $100\times0.3=30$ and $900\times0.8=720$ arrive as $H$, so $750$ arrive as $H$. The share of those that were sent as $H$ is $\frac{30}{750}=0.04$. The sent-$L$ share is $0.96$, and the two shares add to $1$.

questions.stem: For $n>2$, let $a\in\{0,1\}^n$ be a non-zero vector. Suppose that $x$ is chosen uniformly at random from $\{0,1\}^n$. Then, the probability that $\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_ix_i$ is an odd number is ______.

solutionDiagram.alt: For n equals 3 and a equals (1, 0, 1), the eight bit strings grouped into four pairs that differ in the first bit; in every pair one string has x1 plus x3 even and the other odd, so half of the eight are odd.

steps.title: What the question is asking
steps.body: $\{0,1\}^n$ is the set of all bit strings of length $n$, so there are $2^n$ of them. Uniformly at random means each has probability $2^{-n}$, and the probability of an event is its count of strings divided by $2^n$. A number is odd when its remainder on division by 2 (its parity) is 1. In $\sum a_ix_i$ only positions with $a_i=1$ add anything, and each such position adds 1 when $x_i=1$. The rule: flipping one bit $x_j$ with $a_j=1$ changes the sum by exactly 1, so it flips the parity.
steps.tex: \text{sum} \bmod 2 \ \text{changes when } x_j \text{ is flipped and } a_j=1

steps.title: Pair the strings
steps.body: Because $a$ is not zero, pick a position $j$ with $a_j=1$. For each string $x$, let $x'$ be $x$ with bit $j$ flipped. This pairs the $2^n$ strings into $2^{n-1}$ pairs, and in each pair the two sums differ by 1, so exactly one is odd and one is even. The picture shows $n=3$, $a=(1,0,1)$, $j=1$.

steps.title: Count and divide
steps.body: Exactly one string of every pair is odd, so $2^{n-1}$ strings give an odd sum out of $2^n$. Check by direct count: if $a$ has $k\ge1$ ones, an odd number of the $k$ chosen bits must be 1, which can be done in $2^{k-1}$ ways, and the other $n-k$ bits are free, giving $2^{k-1}\cdot2^{n-k}=2^{n-1}$ again. The probability is $\frac12$, independent of $a$ and $n$.

shortcut.body: The question promises a single answer for every non-zero $a$, so test the simplest one, $a=(1,0,\ldots,0)$: the sum is $x_1$, which is odd exactly when $x_1=1$, probability $\frac12$. Safe here because the stem says the answer does not depend on $a$. Thirty seconds.

traps.text: $1-2^{-k}$ (with $k$ ones in $a$): that is the probability that the sum is non-zero, which confuses odd with non-zero. A sum of 2 is non-zero and even.
Answering with something that depends on $a$, such as $k/n$ or $\frac12$ only when $k=1$. The pairing argument works for every non-zero $a$.
$\frac14$, from multiplying two half-chances (one for 'some chosen bit is 1', one for 'it is odd'). Parity is decided by a single flip, so there is only one factor of $\frac12$.

recognize.clues: A uniform choice from all bit strings, a fixed non-zero weight vector, and a question about the parity of a weighted sum, which is a counting question.
recognize.contrast: Independent events would multiply chances of separate conditions; here a single flip decides parity, so a pairing or counting argument is needed rather than a product of halves.

check.body: Try $n=2$ and $a=(1,1)$ by listing: the strings $00,01,10,11$ have sums $0,1,1,2$, so two of four are odd. With $a=(1,0)$ the sums are $0,0,1,1$, again two of four. Both agree with a fixed fraction independent of $a$.

questions.stem: Two numbers are chosen independently and uniformly at random from the set $\{1,2,\ldots,13\}$. The probability (rounded off to 3 decimal places) that their 4-bit (unsigned) binary representations have the same most significant bit is ______.

solutionDiagram.alt: The numbers 1 to 13 in a row with their 4-bit values; 1 to 7 have most significant bit 0 (seven numbers) and 8 to 13 have most significant bit 1 (six numbers); the probability of the same bit is (49 plus 36) over 169, which is 85 over 169.

steps.title: The most significant bit and the rule
steps.body: A 4-bit unsigned number is $b_3b_2b_1b_0$ with value $8b_3+4b_2+2b_1+b_0$. The most significant bit (MSB) is the leftmost bit $b_3$, the one worth 8. So the MSB is 1 exactly when the number is at least 8. Two independent uniform choices from 13 numbers make each ordered pair equally likely, with probability $\frac1{169}$. The MSBs are the same when both are 0 or both are 1; those cases cannot happen together, so their probabilities add.

steps.title: Count the two groups
steps.body: MSB $=0$: numbers 1 to 7, which is 7 numbers. MSB $=1$: numbers 8 to 13, which is 6 numbers. Check: $7+6=13$. The number 0 is not in the set, which is why the groups are unequal.

steps.title: Combine
steps.body: Both 0: $\left(\frac7{13}\right)^2=\frac{49}{169}$. Both 1: $\left(\frac6{13}\right)^2=\frac{36}{169}$. Total $\frac{85}{169}=0.50296\ldots\approx0.503$, inside the key range 0.502 to 0.504.

shortcut.body: Seven numbers have MSB 0 and six have MSB 1, so count ordered pairs: $7^2+6^2=85$ out of $13^2=169$. Since $\frac{169}{2}=84.5<85$, the answer is just above $0.5$, namely $0.503$. About one minute.

traps.text: $0.5$: assuming the MSB is equally likely to be 0 or 1. With the set $\{1,\ldots,13\}$ the split is 7 against 6, so the answer is a little above one half.
$0.510$: counting the number 0 as part of the set (8 zeros, 6 ones out of 14). The set starts at 1.
$0.290$ or $0.213$: using only one of the two cases, $\left(\frac7{13}\right)^2$ or $\left(\frac6{13}\right)^2$, and forgetting the other way the MSBs can agree.

recognize.clues: Two independent uniform picks from a small set of integers and a property of their binary form, which splits the set into groups to count.
recognize.contrast: Treating the bits as fair coins would give one half; the set does not split evenly, so the counts of each group must be used.

check.body: Count the complement. The bits differ when one pick is in the zero group and the other in the one group, in either order: $2\times7\times6=84$ ordered pairs out of $169$. Then the chance of agreement is $1-\frac{84}{169}=\frac{85}{169}$, matching the direct count.

questions.stem: Suppose $Y$ is distributed uniformly in the open interval $(1,6)$. The probability that the polynomial $3x^2+6xY+3Y+6$ has only real roots is (rounded off to 1 decimal place) ______.

solutionDiagram.alt: A number line for Y with the interval 1 to 6 marked. The part from 2 to 6, length 4 out of 5, gives real roots because the discriminant 36 (Y minus 2)(Y plus 1) is non-negative there; the probability is 0.8.

steps.title: Uniform distribution and real roots
steps.body: $Y$ uniform on $(1,6)$ means every value in the interval is equally likely, with density $\frac1{6-1}=\frac15$. The probability that $Y$ falls in a sub-interval is its length divided by 5. A quadratic $ax^2+bx+c$ with real coefficients has only real roots exactly when its discriminant $b^2-4ac$ is at least 0. The plan: turn the condition on the roots into a condition on $Y$, then measure the interval.

steps.title: The discriminant in terms of Y
Solve the inequality inside the interval
steps.body: $\Delta\ge0$ means $(Y-2)(Y+1)\ge0$, so $Y\ge2$ or $Y\le-1$. The interval $(1,6)$ contains no value $\le-1$, so the allowed values are $2\le Y<6$, of length 4. At $Y=2$ the polynomial is $3(x+2)^2$, a double real root, and a single point has probability 0 anyway.

shortcut.body: Divide the discriminant by 12 first: $3Y^2-3Y-6\ge0$ gives $Y^2-Y-2=(Y-2)(Y+1)\ge0$. Only $Y\ge2$ matters inside $(1,6)$, so $\frac{6-2}{5}=0.8$. About two minutes.

traps.text: $0.2$: the probability of complex roots, $\frac{2-1}{5}$, the complement of what is asked.
$0$: taking $b=6$ instead of $6Y$ (forgetting that $Y$ multiplies $x$). Then $\Delta=36-12(3Y+6)<0$ for all $Y>0$ and the answer looks like zero.
$0.6$: solving $Y^2-Y-2\ge0$ with a wrong root (such as $Y\ge3$), which gives $\frac{6-3}{5}$. Factor and expand back to check: $(Y-2)(Y+1)=Y^2-Y-2$.

recognize.clues: A parameter that is uniform on an open interval, entering the coefficients of a polynomial, and a question about a property of the roots.
recognize.contrast: This is not a discrete count of cases: the probability is a length ratio on a continuum, so a single boundary point carries no weight.

check.body: Spot checks. At $Y=3$ the polynomial is $3x^2+18x+15$ with discriminant $324-180=144>0$, real. At $Y=1.5$ it is $3x^2+9x+10.5$ with discriminant $81-126<0$, complex. At the boundary $Y=2$ it is $3x^2+12x+12$ with discriminant $0$. This puts the switch point at $2$, inside the interval.

questions.stem: Two people, $P$ and $Q$, decide to independently roll two identical dice, each with 6 faces, numbered 1 to 6. The person with the lower number wins. In case of a tie, they roll the dice repeatedly until there is no tie. Define a trial as a throw of the dice by $P$ and $Q$. Assume that all 6 numbers on each dice are equi-probable and that all trials are independent. The probability (rounded to 3 decimal places) that one of them wins on the third trial is ______.

solutionDiagram.alt: Three trials in a row: trial 1 is a tie with probability 1/6, trial 2 is a tie with probability 1/6, trial 3 has a winner with probability 5/6, and the product is 5/216, about 0.023.

steps.title: Trials, ties and the multiplication rule
steps.body: One trial is one throw by both players. It ends in a tie when both show the same number; otherwise the lower number wins. The game stops at the first trial that is not a tie. Because the trials are independent, the probability of a specific run of outcomes is the product of the probabilities of the individual trials. Someone wins on the third trial exactly when trial 1 is a tie, trial 2 is a tie and trial 3 is not a tie.

steps.title: Probability of a tie in one trial
steps.body: There are $6\times6=36$ equally likely pairs of faces, and 6 of them are ties (1,1), (2,2), ..., (6,6). So $\Pr(\text{tie})=\frac6{36}=\frac16$ and $\Pr(\text{no tie})=\frac56$.

steps.title: Multiply
steps.body: $\left(\frac16\right)\left(\frac16\right)\left(\frac56\right)=\frac5{216}=0.0231\ldots\approx0.023$, inside the key range 0.021 to 0.024.

shortcut.body: This is a geometric probability: the first success after $k-1$ failures has chance $q^{k-1}(1-q)$ with $q=\frac16$. So $\frac{5}{6^3}=\frac5{216}$. Since $\frac5{200}=0.025$, the answer is a little less: $0.023$. About thirty seconds.

traps.text: $0.139$: that is $\frac16\cdot\frac56$, winning on the second trial. Read the trial number again.
$0.005$: $\left(\frac16\right)^3$ makes all three trials ties, in which case nobody wins at all.
$0.116$ from $\left(\frac56\right)^2\frac16$: this makes the first two trials decisive, but the game would have ended at trial 1.

recognize.clues: The game repeats independent trials until the first decisive one, and the question asks for the first success on a named trial number. That wording is the first-success (geometric) pattern.
recognize.contrast: A binomial asks for a count of successes in a fixed number of trials; here the number of trials is not fixed, and what matters is on which trial the first success lands.

check.body: Add the chances of the game ending on trial 1, 2, 3, and so on: with tie chance $q$ they form a geometric series $\sum_{k\ge1}q^{k-1}(1-q)$ that must total 1. For $q=\frac16$ the first three terms are $\frac56$, $\frac5{36}$ and the trial-3 term, and the remaining tail $q^3$ makes the total exactly 1, which fits the trial-3 value found.

questions.stem: Consider Guwahati ($G$) and Delhi ($D$) whose temperatures can be classified as high ($H$), medium ($M$) and low ($L$). Let $P(H_G)$ denote the probability that Guwahati has high temperature. Similarly, $P(M_G)$ and $P(L_G)$ denotes the probability of Guwahati having medium and low temperatures respectively. Similarly, we use $P(H_D)$, $P(M_D)$ and $P(L_D)$ for Delhi. The following table gives the conditional probabilities for Delhi's temperature given Guwahati's temperature. Consider the first row in the table above. The first entry denotes that if Guwahati has high temperature ($H_G$) then the probability of Delhi also having a high temperature ($H_D$) is $0.40$; i.e., $P(H_D\mid H_G)=0.40$. Similarly, the next two entries are $P(M_D\mid H_G)=0.48$ and $P(L_D\mid H_G)=0.12$. Similarly for the other rows. If it is known that $P(H_G)=0.2$, $P(M_G)=0.5$, and $P(L_G)=0.3$, then the probability (correct to two decimal places) that Guwahati has high temperature given that Delhi has high temperature is ______.

solutionDiagram.alt: Probability tree: Guwahati high, medium or low with priors 0.2, 0.5, 0.3 then Delhi high with 0.40, 0.10, 0.01, giving 0.080, 0.050, 0.003; the posterior for Guwahati high is 0.080 over 0.133, about 0.60.

steps.title: Which conditional probability is given, and which is wanted
steps.body: A conditional probability $P(A\mid B)$ is the chance of $A$ when $B$ is known to have happened. The table gives Delhi's temperature given Guwahati's, $P(D\mid G)$. The question needs the reverse, $P(H_G\mid H_D)$. Bayes' rule reverses a conditional: multiply the given conditional by the prior of the condition, then divide by the total chance of the new condition. That total comes from total probability: add over every Guwahati temperature.

steps.title: Chance of Delhi high through each Guwahati state
steps.body: Use only the $H_D$ column. Guwahati high: $0.40\times0.2=0.080$. Guwahati medium: $0.10\times0.5=0.050$. Guwahati low: $0.01\times0.3=0.003$.

steps.title: Apply Bayes
steps.body: The part of $0.133$ that came through Guwahati high is $0.080$, so $P(H_G\mid H_D)=\frac{0.080}{0.133}=0.6015\ldots\approx0.60$, inside the key range 0.60 to 0.62.

shortcut.body: Read down the $H_D$ column only and weight each entry by the prior: $0.08,\ 0.05,\ 0.003$. Answer: $0.08/0.133\approx0.6$. About one minute; no other column enters.

traps.text: $0.40$: reading the table entry $P(H_D\mid H_G)$ as the answer. It conditions in the opposite direction.
$0.08$ or $0.2$: stopping at the joint probability, or at the prior $P(H_G)$. Divide by $P(H_D)=0.133$.
$0.133$: that is the denominator $P(H_D)$ itself, the chance Delhi is high, not the posterior.

recognize.clues: The table lists the probability of one city given the other, while the question asks for the reverse direction, and priors for the conditioning city are supplied. Reversing a conditional with priors is the signal.
recognize.contrast: Plain conditional probability reads one entry of the table directly; here the wanted direction is not in the table, so the denominator must be built by total probability.

check.body: Compute the other two posteriors with the same denominator: $0.050/0.133$ for medium and $0.003/0.133$ for low. All three shares must add up to 1, and the three numerators together must equal the denominator. Each posterior also lies between 0 and 1.

questions.stem: P and Q are considering to apply for a job. The probability that P applies for the job is $\frac14$, the probability that P applies for the job given that Q applies for the job is $\frac12$, and the probability that Q applies for the job given that P applies for the job is $\frac13$. Then the probability that P does not apply for the job given that Q does not apply for the job is

solutionDiagram.alt: A two by two table of joint probabilities: P and Q both apply 1/12, only P 1/6, only Q 1/12, neither 2/3, with row totals 1/4 and 3/4 and column totals 1/6 and 5/6. The answer is the neither cell 2/3 divided by the Q-does-not-apply column total 5/6, which is 4/5.

steps.title: Events and conditional probability
steps.body: Let $P$ be the event that P applies and $Q$ the event that Q applies; a bar means the opposite event. The conditional probability $\Pr(X\mid Y)=\Pr(X\cap Y)/\Pr(Y)$ is the chance of $X$ once $Y$ is known to hold. Rearranged, it gives the joint probability $\Pr(X\cap Y)=\Pr(X\mid Y)\Pr(Y)$. Plan: use the three given numbers to find the whole 2-by-2 table of joint probabilities, then read off the conditional probability asked for.

steps.title: Both apply
steps.body: From $\Pr(Q\mid P)=\frac13$ and $\Pr(P)=\frac14$: $\Pr(P\cap Q)=\frac13\cdot\frac14=\frac1{12}$.

steps.title: Q applies
steps.body: From $\Pr(P\mid Q)=\frac12$: $\Pr(Q)=\Pr(P\cap Q)/\Pr(P\mid Q)=\frac{1/12}{1/2}=\frac16$. Hence $\Pr(\bar Q)=\frac56$.

steps.title: Fill in the table
steps.body: $\Pr(P\cap\bar Q)=\frac14-\frac1{12}=\frac16$. $\Pr(\bar P\cap Q)=\frac16-\frac1{12}=\frac1{12}$. $\Pr(\bar P\cap\bar Q)=1-\frac1{12}-\frac16-\frac1{12}=\frac23$. The four cells add to 1.

steps.title: Conditional on Q not applying
steps.body: $\Pr(\bar P\mid\bar Q)=\frac{\Pr(\bar P\cap\bar Q)}{\Pr(\bar Q)}=\frac{2/3}{5/6}=\frac45$. That is option A.

shortcut.body: Draw the 2-by-2 table: $\Pr(P\cap Q)=\frac1{12}$ first, then $\Pr(Q)=\frac16$ from the second conditional, and the other cells follow by subtraction from $\frac14$, $\frac16$ and $1$. The bottom-right cell $\frac23$ over the column total $\frac56$ is $\frac45$. About two minutes.

traps.text: $\frac56$ is $\Pr(\bar Q)$, the denominator. The question asks for the share of the 'Q does not apply' column in which P also does not apply.
$\frac78$ equals $1-\frac12\cdot\frac14$, from multiplying $\Pr(P\mid Q)$ by $\Pr(P)$. The joint probability needs $\Pr(P\mid Q)\times\Pr(Q)$, with $\Pr(Q)=\frac16$ not $\frac14$.
$\frac{11}{12}$ is $1-\Pr(P\cap Q)$, the chance that they do not both apply. It is not conditioned on Q staying out.

recognize.clues: Three probabilities are given, two of them conditional in opposite directions, and the target is again a conditional on a complement event. All of that is about moving between joint and conditional probabilities.
recognize.contrast: Independence would let you multiply the marginals, but the two conditionals differ from the marginal $\frac14$, so P and Q are not independent and the joint must be recovered from the conditionals.

check.body: Verify the table against all three given numbers: $\Pr(P)=\frac1{12}+\frac16=\frac14$, $\Pr(P\mid Q)=\frac{1/12}{1/6}=\frac12$ and $\Pr(Q\mid P)=\frac{1/12}{1/4}=\frac13$. Also confirm the four cells sum to 1.

questions.stem: For any discrete random variable $X$, with probability mass function $P(X=j)=p_j$, $p_j\ge0$, $j\in\{0,\ldots,N\}$, and $\sum_{j=0}^{N}p_j=1$, define the polynomial function $g_X(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{N}p_jz^j$. For a certain discrete random variable $Y$, there exists a scalar $\beta\in[0,1]$ such that $g_Y(z)=(1-\beta+\beta z)^N$. The expectation of $Y$ is
options: Not expressible in terms of $N$ and $\beta$ alone

steps.title: The generating polynomial and the mean
steps.body: The polynomial $g_X(z)=\sum_j p_jz^j$ stores the whole probability mass function: the coefficient of $z^j$ is $p_j$. The expectation (mean) of $X$ is $E[X]=\sum_j j\,p_j$. Differentiate once: $g_X'(z)=\sum_j j\,p_jz^{j-1}$. Put $z=1$ and every power of $z$ becomes 1, so $g_X'(1)=\sum_j jp_j$. The rule: the mean is the derivative of $g_X$ at $z=1$.

steps.title: Differentiate the given polynomial
steps.body: For $g_Y(z)=(1-\beta+\beta z)^N$, the chain rule gives $g_Y'(z)=N\beta\,(1-\beta+\beta z)^{N-1}$. At $z=1$ the bracket is $1-\beta+\beta=1$, so $g_Y'(1)=N\beta$.

steps.title: Cross-check by recognising the distribution
steps.body: The binomial theorem expands $(1-\beta+\beta z)^N=\sum_j\binom Nj\beta^j(1-\beta)^{N-j}z^j$. So $p_j=\binom Nj\beta^j(1-\beta)^{N-j}$: $Y$ is binomial with $N$ trials and success probability $\beta$, whose mean is $N\beta$. Answer: option B.

shortcut.body: $(1-\beta+\beta z)^N$ is the binomial generating polynomial (failure part plus success part times $z$, to the power $N$). A binomial with $N$ trials and success probability $\beta$ has mean $N\beta$. Fifteen seconds.

traps.text: $N\beta(1-\beta)$ is the variance of the binomial, not the mean. Variance would need the second derivative of $g$ at 1.
$N(1-\beta)$ is the expected number of failures. The power of $z$ counts successes, since $\beta$ multiplies $z$.
The polynomial determines every $p_j$, so $E[Y]$ is fully fixed by $N$ and $\beta$; nothing is hidden.

recognize.clues: A polynomial whose coefficients are the probabilities is given, and the quantity asked is an expectation. Differentiating the generating polynomial at 1 produces the mean.
recognize.contrast: The binomial variance $N\beta(1-\beta)$ looks similar but needs the second derivative as well; the mean needs only the first derivative at 1.

check.body: Test with $N=1$: the polynomial is $1-\beta+\beta z$, so $Y$ is 1 with chance $\beta$ and 0 otherwise, and its mean is plainly $\beta$. Also at $\beta=1$ all mass sits at $j=N$, so the mean must be $N$. The formula must meet both.

questions.stem: If a random variable $X$ has a Poisson distribution with mean $5$, then the expectation $E[(X+2)^2]$ equals ______.

steps.title: The Poisson distribution and linearity
steps.body: A Poisson variable counts events in a fixed interval. Its single parameter $\lambda$ is both its mean and its variance, so here $E[X]=5$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X)=5$. Variance is $\mathrm{Var}(X)=E[X^2]-(E[X])^2$, so $E[X^2]=\mathrm{Var}(X)+(E[X])^2$. Expectation is linear: $E[aX+b]=aE[X]+b$ and expectations of sums add. The plan: expand the square, then apply these.

steps.title: Insert the numbers
steps.body: $E[X^2]=5+25=30$ and $4E[X]=20$. Adding, $30+20+4=54$. A numerical sum of the Poisson probabilities, $\sum_k(k+2)^2e^{-5}5^k/k!$, gives $54$ too.

shortcut.body: Shift trick: $E[(X+2)^2]=\mathrm{Var}(X+2)+(E[X+2])^2$. Adding a constant leaves the variance at $5$, and the mean becomes $7$, so $5+49=54$. Twenty seconds.

traps.text: $49$: squaring the mean, $(E[X]+2)^2$. In general $E[Z^2]\ne(E[Z])^2$; the gap is the variance, $5$ here.
$30$: giving $E[X^2]$ and forgetting the $4X+4$ part of the expansion.
$29$: using $E[X^2]=\lambda=5$ instead of $\lambda+\lambda^2=30$, then $5+20+4$.

recognize.clues: The variable is named Poisson with a given mean, and the target is the expectation of a polynomial in it. Only the mean and variance of the Poisson are needed.
recognize.contrast: A binomial also has a mean and variance, but they differ in form; for the Poisson they are the same number, which is what makes $E[X^2]$ immediate.

check.body: Test the general formula at an extreme: with mean $\lambda=0$ the variable is always $0$, so $E[(X+2)^2]=4$. The expression $E[X^2]+4E[X]+4=\lambda^2+5\lambda+4$ gives $4$ at $\lambda=0$, and at $\lambda=5$ it factors as $(\lambda+1)(\lambda+4)$.

questions.stem: Let $X$ be a Gaussian random variable with mean $0$ and variance $\sigma^2$. Let $Y=\max(X,0)$ where $\max(a,b)$ is the maximum of $a$ and $b$. The median of $Y$ is ______.

solutionDiagram.alt: Graph of the distribution function of Y equals max(X, 0): zero for negative y, a jump of 0.5 at y equals 0, then rising to 1; the dashed line at 0.5 meets the graph at y equals 0, so the median is 0.

steps.title: Median and the distribution function
steps.body: The median of a random variable is a middle value: at least half of the probability lies at or below it, and at least half lies at or above it. In terms of the distribution function $F(y)=\Pr(Y\le y)$, the median is the smallest $m$ with $F(m)\ge\frac12$. This works even when the variable has no density, as here.

steps.title: The distribution of Y = max(X, 0)
steps.body: $Y$ equals $X$ when $X>0$ and equals $0$ otherwise. A Gaussian with mean 0 is symmetric about 0, so $\Pr(X\le0)=\frac12$. Therefore $\Pr(Y=0)=\frac12$: half of the probability sits in a single point at 0. For $y<0$, $F(y)=0$; for $y\ge0$, $F(y)=\Pr(X\le y)=\Phi(y/\sigma)$, which is $\frac12$ at $y=0$ and larger beyond.

steps.title: Read off the median
steps.body: For every $y<0$, $F(y)=0<\frac12$, and $F(0)=\frac12$. So the smallest $m$ with $F(m)\ge\frac12$ is $m=0$; the check on the other side holds too, since $\Pr(Y\ge0)=1$. The median is $0$ whatever $\sigma$ is.

shortcut.body: Every negative value of $X$ is turned into $0$, so half of the probability mass is exactly at $0$. The middle value is therefore $0$, independent of $\sigma$. Ten seconds.

traps.text: $0.6745\,\sigma$: the median of $|X|$, where all the negative mass is folded onto the positive side. Here it is piled at $0$ instead.
$\sigma/\sqrt{2\pi}\approx0.399\,\sigma$: the mean of $Y$, not its median. The mean and median differ because $Y$ is lopsided.
Answering in terms of $\sigma$ at all: the median of $X$ is $0$, and the clipping keeps the half of the mass at or below 0 on the point $0$.

recognize.clues: A new variable is made by clipping a symmetric Gaussian with a maximum, and the question asks for its median. Clipping piles probability on one point, so the distribution function must be used.
recognize.contrast: The mean of $Y$ depends on $\sigma$ and is positive; the median does not, because the median only needs where half of the mass is reached.

check.body: Take $\sigma=1$ and imagine $1000$ draws of $Y$: about $500$ are clipped to exactly $0$ and the rest are positive, so the middle draw sits at $0$. A point just below, such as $-0.1$, has $F(-0.1)=0$, under one half, so no negative number can be the median.

variation.stem: Let $X$ be a Gaussian random variable with mean $0$ and variance $\sigma^2>0$, and let $Y=\max(X,1)$. The median of $Y$ is ______.
variation.explanation: For $y<1$ the distribution function is $0$. At $y=1$ it equals $\Pr(X\le1)$, which exceeds $\frac12$ because $X$ is symmetric about $0<1$. So the first point where it reaches $\frac12$ is $1$.
